drills.q: Explain an RLM in one sentence to an interviewer.
drills.a: It keeps a long prompt outside the model as a programmable data environment and lets the model inspect, decompose, and recursively solve selected slices instead of processing the entire prompt in one context.

drills.q: Why does a 1M-token context window not eliminate context engineering?
drills.a: Nominal capacity is not uniform reasoning quality. Attention dilution and context rot can reduce recall or synthesis quality while the input still fits, and cost/latency remain material.

drills.q: Contrast RLM with a vector database retriever.
drills.a: A vector retriever selects chunks using an index and similarity metric. An RLM exposes the prompt as data that the model can search, slice, inspect, and recursively process, which can support exact filters and task-specific exploration without pre-indexing.

drills.q: Design the environment API for an RLM processing 5,000 support tickets.
drills.a: Expose bounded peek, regex/keyword search, partition by ticket, typed child calls, aggregation, and provenance. Deny arbitrary filesystem/network access; cap depth, fan-out, tokens, wall time, and output size.

drills.q: Why is just recursively calling the model on every chunk a bad design?
drills.a: It creates a fan-out cost explosion and may duplicate work. First filter or partition programmatically, then call only on relevant slices, use structured outputs, parallelize safely, and enforce cumulative budgets.

drills.q: What observability proves an RLM is bounded?
drills.a: Trace parent-child call relationships and record recursion depth, fan-out, selected byte/token ranges, child prompt/completion tokens, cumulative cost, wall time, cancellations, retries, and final aggregation status.

drills.q: A child call times out after its siblings completed. What should the parent do?
drills.a: Represent the timeout as a typed partial failure, preserve which slice was missing, apply a policy such as retry once or return a bounded incomplete result, and never silently treat missing evidence as negative evidence.

drills.q: When would RLM be worse than RAG?
drills.a: For a stable corpus with high reuse, a well-tuned retriever and cache may be cheaper and faster. RLM adds model-call orchestration and can repeatedly scan data; use it when programmatic exploration or long-context degradation is the actual bottleneck.

drills.q: How do you prevent a malicious document from turning an RLM into an agent?
drills.a: Keep the environment capabilities narrow and deterministic, mark document text as untrusted data, validate all tool and child-call arguments outside the model, sandbox code, deny arbitrary egress, and apply hard budgets and audit logging.

drills.q: How would you evaluate RLM against compaction fairly?
drills.a: Use identical task inputs, model/provider, output contract, and quality rubric. Compare answer correctness and evidence coverage while separately reporting model calls, input/output tokens, wall time, cache effects, failure rate, and human review cost.

drills.q: Why can RLM improve a shorter prompt too, not just an oversized one?
drills.a: It can enforce deliberate programmatic search and decomposition instead of asking attention to scan everything. The benefit is selective computation and structure, not merely fitting beyond a context limit.

drills.q: What is the principal-level migration path from a vanilla long-context system to RLM?
drills.a: Instrument context-length versus quality first, identify tasks with context rot, add a read-only external environment and deterministic slice tools, introduce typed child calls behind a feature flag, compare against the old path on a fixed eval set, then expand only if quality/cost/latency justify the operational complexity.
